PFGT-UIE — see the results yourself

Underwater photo enhancement. Every image below is one the model was never trained on, so these are fair tests, not memorised answers. The panel with the brighter caption is the best-performing version.

What you are looking at. Each row is one underwater photograph. Left to right: the original murky photo, then what three different versions of our software produced, then the “correct” answer a human editor made by hand. The closer our result looks to that last image, the better.

The headline, stated plainly: tonight’s change did not work. Averaged over all 89 test photos, tonight’s version scores 24.50 — lower than last session’s 24.80. (The original first version scored 24.42.) Higher is better, so last session’s version is still the best one, and it is the one left installed on the machine. For scale: a 1-point gain is a difference most people can see, so the 0.30-point drop here is small enough that you will struggle to spot it by eye — but it is a drop, not a gain, and it is being reported as one.

What tonight was trying to do. The software has a component whose only job is to fix the overall colour tint of a photo — the blue-green wash you get underwater. It was built last session but turned out to be barely doing anything, so tonight it was given a direct instruction to do that job properly.

Why it did not help — and why that is still worth knowing. Before training, I measured how much of that colour tint is actually predictable from the murky photo alone. The answer is: not much. The “correct” images were made by a human editor by hand, and a lot of their colour reflects that person’s taste rather than anything recoverable from the original photograph. Pushing the software harder to guess it simply made it worse at everything else. That measurement is the most useful result of the night: it shows this particular avenue was largely a dead end, which means nobody needs to spend more time on it.

Compared against the original first version, tonight’s is visibly better on 39 of the 89 test photos, about the same on 14, and worse on 36. Both the wins and the losses are shown below — the losses are not hidden.
